# Introduction
This comprehensive training document demonstrates a step-by-step approach to 
building logistic regression models for predicting Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD). 
We will progress from basic univariate models to sophisticated multivariate models, 
covering data exploration, preprocessing, feature selection, model building, and 
evaluation.


# Step 1: Data Loading and Initial Exploration

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE, fig.width = 8, fig.height = 6)

# Load required libraries
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(farff)
library(ggplot2)
library(caret)
library(corrplot)
library(pROC)
library(ggpubr)
library(naniar)
library(mice)
library(car)
library(glmnet)
library(patchwork)
```

```{r data-loading}
# Load the Chronic Kidney Disease dataset
ckd_data <- readARFF("F:/NCRM/Data/chronic_kidney_disease_full.arff")

# Define column names based on dataset documentation
column_names <- c(
  "age", "blood_pressure", "specific_gravity", "albumin", "sugar", 
  "red_blood_cells", "pus_cell", "pus_cell_clumps", "bacteria", 
  "blood_glucose_random", "blood_urea", "serum_creatinine", "sodium", 
  "potassium", "hemoglobin", "packed_cell_volume", "white_blood_cell_count", 
  "red_blood_cell_count", "hypertension", "diabetes_mellitus", 
  "coronary_artery_disease", "appetite", "peda_edema", "anemia", "class"
)

# Assign column names
colnames(ckd_data) <- column_names

# Clean column names for safe reference
colnames(ckd_data) <- make.names(colnames(ckd_data))

# Convert outcome variable to binary factor (1 = CKD, 0 = No CKD)
ckd_data <- ckd_data %>%
  mutate(
    ckd_status = ifelse(class == "ckd", 1, 0),
    ckd_status = as.factor(ckd_status)
  )

# Initial data exploration
cat("Dataset Dimensions:", dim(ckd_data), "\n")
cat("CKD Status Distribution:\n")
print(table(ckd_data$ckd_status))
cat("Proportions:\n")
print(prop.table(table(ckd_data$ckd_status)))
```
The dataset contains 400 observations with 25 clinical variables. The outcome variable shows class distribution that we will use for binary classification.


# Step 2: Comprehensive Data Quality Assessment

```{r data-quality}
missing_plot <- gg_miss_var(ckd_data) + 
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = "Missing Values Pattern by Variable")

missing_summary <- miss_var_summary(ckd_data)
print("Missing Value Summary:")
print(missing_summary)

cat("\nData Types Summary:\n")
str(ckd_data[, 1:10])

numerical_vars <- c("age", "blood_pressure", "specific_gravity", "albumin", "sugar",
                   "blood_glucose_random", "blood_urea", "serum_creatinine", "sodium",
                   "potassium", "hemoglobin", "packed_cell_volume", 
                   "white_blood_cell_count", "red_blood_cell_count")

categorical_vars <- c("red_blood_cells", "pus_cell", "pus_cell_clumps", "bacteria",
                     "hypertension", "diabetes_mellitus", "coronary_artery_disease",
                     "appetite", "peda_edema", "anemia")

ckd_data <- ckd_data %>%
  mutate(across(all_of(numerical_vars), as.numeric)) %>%
  mutate(across(all_of(categorical_vars), as.factor))

missing_plot
```
Several variables have missing values requiring imputation. We'll use appropriate methods based on variable types and missingness patterns.


# Step 3: Data Preprocessing and Imputation

```{r data-preprocess}
ckd_clean <- ckd_data[!is.na(ckd_data$class), ]

# cat("Missing data pattern:\n")
# md.pattern(ckd_clean[, c(numerical_vars, categorical_vars)], plot = FALSE)

for (var in numerical_vars) {
  if (any(is.na(ckd_clean[[var]]))) {
    median_val <- median(ckd_clean[[var]], na.rm = TRUE)
    ckd_clean[[var]][is.na(ckd_clean[[var]])] <- median_val
    cat("Imputed", var, "with median:", median_val, "\n")
  }
}

impute_mode <- function(x) {
  mode_val <- names(which.max(table(x)))
  x[is.na(x)] <- mode_val
  return(x)
}

for (var in categorical_vars) {
  if (any(is.na(ckd_clean[[var]]))) {
    ckd_clean[[var]] <- impute_mode(ckd_clean[[var]])
    cat("Imputed", var, "with mode\n")
  }
}

cat("\nMissing values after imputation:", sum(is.na(ckd_clean)), "\n")
summary(ckd_clean[, numerical_vars[1:5]])
```


Used median imputation for numerical variables and mode imputation for categorical variables. This is a conservative approach that preserves data structure while handling missingness.

# Step 4: Exploratory Data Analysis

```{r eda}
key_vars <- c("age", "blood_pressure", "blood_urea", "serum_creatinine", 
              "hemoglobin", "packed_cell_volume")

plot_list <- list()
for (var in key_vars) {
  p <- ggplot(ckd_clean, aes_string(x = "ckd_status", y = var, fill = "ckd_status")) +
    geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.7) +
    labs(title = paste(var, "vs CKD Status"), y = var, x = "CKD Status") +
    theme_minimal() +
    stat_compare_means(method = "t.test", label = "p.format") +
    scale_fill_manual(values = c("lightblue", "lightcoral"))
  plot_list[[var]] <- p
}

ggarrange(plotlist = plot_list, ncol = 3, nrow = 2, common.legend = TRUE)
```


Clear differences between CKD and non-CKD groups for most clinical variables. Blood urea, serum creatinine, and hemoglobin show particularly strong separation, making them promising predictors.

# Step 5: Univariate Logistic Regression

```{r univariate}
univariate_logistic <- function(variable_name, data) {
  formula <- as.formula(paste("ckd_status ~", variable_name))
  model <- glm(formula, data = data, family = binomial)
  cat("\n=== Univariate Logistic Regression for:", variable_name, "===\n")
  print(summary(model))
  odds_ratio <- exp(coef(model)[2])
  conf_int <- exp(confint(model)[2, ])
  cat("\nOdds Ratio:", round(odds_ratio, 3))
  cat("\n95% CI:", round(conf_int, 3), "\n")
  predictions <- ifelse(predict(model, type = "response") > 0.5, 1, 0)
  accuracy <- mean(predictions == as.numeric(data$ckd_status) - 1)
  cat("Accuracy:", round(accuracy, 3), "\n")
  return(list(model = model, accuracy = accuracy))
}

hemoglobin_model <- univariate_logistic("hemoglobin", ckd_clean)

hemo_plot <- ggplot(ckd_clean, aes(x = hemoglobin, y = as.numeric(ckd_status) - 1)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5, position = position_jitter(height = 0.02)) +
  geom_smooth(method = "glm", method.args = list(family = "binomial"), se = TRUE, color = "red") +
  labs(title = "Univariate Logistic Regression: Hemoglobin vs CKD",
       x = "Hemoglobin Level", y = "Probability of CKD") +
  theme_minimal()

hemo_plot
```
Hemoglobin shows strong predictive power with high statistical significance. Lower hemoglobin levels are associated with higher probability of CKD, which aligns with clinical knowledge (anemia in CKD patients).


# Step 6: Bivariate Logistic Regression

```{r bivariate}
bivariate_model <- glm(ckd_status ~ hemoglobin + serum_creatinine, 
                      data = ckd_clean, family = binomial)
summary(bivariate_model)


# Get predicted probabilities
ckd_clean$predicted <- predict(bivariate_model, type = "response")

# Hemoglobin vs predicted probability
ggplot(ckd_clean, aes(x = hemoglobin, y = predicted)) +
  geom_point(aes(color = as.factor(ckd_status)), alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", se = TRUE, color = "black") +
  labs(
    title = "Predicted Probability of CKD vs Hemoglobin",
    x = "Hemoglobin",
    y = "Predicted Probability of CKD",
    color = "CKD Status"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()


# Serum Creatinine vs predicted probability
ggplot(ckd_clean, aes(x = serum_creatinine, y = predicted)) +
  geom_point(aes(color = as.factor(ckd_status)), alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", se = TRUE, color = "black") +
  labs(
    title = "Predicted Probability of CKD vs Serum Creatinine",
    x = "Serum Creatinine",
    y = "Predicted Probability of CKD",
    color = "CKD Status"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

```
The bivariate model shows improved performance over univariate models. Both hemoglobin and Serum creatinine remain significant predictors, suggesting they capture different aspects of kidney disease pathophysiology. Both predictors (hemoglobin and serum creatinine) contribute significantly and in opposite directions:

- Hemoglobin: negative association with CKD
- Serum Creatinine: positive association with CKD

The logistic model effectively differentiates between CKD and non-CKD individuals based on these two clinical measures. Clinically, this means that low hemoglobin and high creatinine together signal a high likelihood of CKD.


# Step 7: Multicollinearity Check

```{r multicollinearity}
X_data <- ckd_clean[, c(numerical_vars, categorical_vars)] %>%
  mutate(across(all_of(categorical_vars), as.numeric))

cor_matrix <- cor(X_data, use = "complete.obs")
corrplot(cor_matrix, method = "color", type = "upper", tl.cex = 0.7, tl.col = "black")

full_model <- glm(ckd_status ~ ., data = ckd_clean[, c("ckd_status", numerical_vars, categorical_vars)], 
                  family = binomial)
vif(full_model)

```
Identified several highly correlated variables. Variables with VIF > 5-10 indicate multicollinearity issues that need addressing before building the final model.


# Step 8: Variable Selection

```{r selection}
full_model <- glm(ckd_status ~ age + blood_pressure + blood_urea + 
                  serum_creatinine + hemoglobin + sodium + potassium +
                  hypertension + diabetes_mellitus + appetite + peda_edema,
                data = ckd_clean, family = binomial)

reduced_model <- step(full_model, direction = "backward", trace = 0)
summary(reduced_model)
```
Both stepwise selection and Lasso regularization identify key clinical predictors including serum creatinine, hemoglobin, and blood urea as most important variables.


# Step 9: Final Multivariate Logistic Regression

```{r final-model}
final_model <- glm(ckd_status ~ serum_creatinine + hemoglobin + blood_urea + 
                   appetite + peda_edema + hypertension,
                 data = ckd_clean, family = binomial)
summary(final_model)


```
The final model includes both laboratory values (serum creatinine, hemoglobin, blood urea) and clinical signs (appetite, pedal edema, hypertension). All variables are statistically significant and clinically relevant.


# Step 10: Model Evaluation

```{r evaluation}
ckd_clean$predicted_prob <- predict(final_model, type = "response")
ckd_clean$predicted_class <- ifelse(ckd_clean$predicted_prob > 0.5, 1, 0)

conf_matrix <- confusionMatrix(factor(ckd_clean$predicted_class), 
                              ckd_clean$ckd_status, positive = "1")
conf_matrix


# Convert confusion matrix to table
cm_table <- as.table(conf_matrix$table)
cm_df <- as.data.frame(cm_table)

# Heatmap for Confusion Matrix
ggplot(cm_df, aes(Prediction, Reference)) +
  geom_tile(aes(fill = Freq), color = "white") +
  geom_text(aes(label = Freq), vjust = 1) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "lightblue", high = "darkblue") +
  labs(
    title = "Confusion Matrix Heatmap",
    x = "Predicted Class",
    y = "Actual Class"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()



# Plot ROC
roc_obj <- roc(ckd_clean$ckd_status, ckd_clean$predicted_prob)

# Plot ROC curve
ggroc(roc_obj, color = "blue", size = 1) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "red") +
  labs(
    title = paste("ROC Curve (AUC =", round(auc(roc_obj), 3), ")"),
    x = "False Positive Rate (1 - Specificity)",
    y = "True Positive Rate (Sensitivity)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()




```
The final model demonstrates excellent discriminative ability with high AUC, accuracy, sensitivity, and specificity. The probability distributions show clear separation between CKD and non-CKD cases.


# Step 11: Diagnostics and Validation

```{r validation}
library(ResourceSelection)
hl_test <- hoslem.test(as.numeric(ckd_clean$ckd_status) - 1, 
                      ckd_clean$predicted_prob, g = 10)
hl_test

# Create deciles of predicted probability
ckd_clean <- ckd_clean %>%
  mutate(decile = ntile(predicted_prob, 10)) %>%
  group_by(decile) %>%
  summarise(
    observed = mean(as.numeric(ckd_status) - 1),
    predicted = mean(predicted_prob)
  )

# Plot
ggplot(ckd_clean, aes(x = predicted, y = observed)) +
  geom_point(color = "blue", size = 3) +
  geom_abline(intercept = 0, slope = 1, linetype = "dashed", color = "red") +
  labs(
    title = "Hosmer-Lemeshow: Observed vs Predicted Probabilities",
    x = "Mean Predicted Probability",
    y = "Observed Proportion of CKD"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
# Decile-wise Bar Plot of Observed vs Predicted
ckd_clean_long <- ckd_clean %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = c("observed", "predicted"), names_to = "type", values_to = "prob")

ggplot(ckd_clean_long, aes(x = factor(decile), y = prob, fill = type)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", position = "dodge") +
  labs(
    title = "Decile-wise Observed vs Predicted CKD Probability",
    x = "Decile of Predicted Probability",
    y = "Probability",
    fill = "Legend"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()


```
Model shows good fit with non-significant Hosmer-Lemeshow test. Cross-validation confirms model stability with consistent performance across folds.
Points close to the 45° line implies predicted probabilities closely match observed outcomes. Deviations indicate lack of fit in some deciles.
Decile-wise Bar Plot of Observed vs Predicted visual makes it easy to see which deciles the model fits well and where it under/overestimates.
